linguisticFindings.detail: Two core units separately teach sleeping and numb limbs. All 12 structured examples, including the added figurative unit, were read. The hand/foot meaning is not interpreted as a limb literally sleeping; numb is wider and awake is not imposed as its antonym.

Asleep is a state adjective usually following a linking verb; sleeping can modify a noun or form a progressive verb phrase. Sleepy is the feeling of wanting sleep, not a blanket synonym for already asleep.

Fresh Etymonline supports on slæpe and aslepe with their sleep-state meanings. The revised caveat now describes simplified history, not merely modern construction, and expressly rejects parsing the opening as modern article a.

The revised foot example makes I the person sitting. The added club-leaders example naturally uses asleep at the wheel for inattention and is distinct from literal driving/sleeping. The note warns that context decides between those uses; this extension is not a new core meaning requiring a physical-sleep reading.

freshPages.summary: Asleep continues Old English on slæpe, with Middle English forms including aslepe, for being or entering sleep. The old expression and its meaning support the historical account. Modern article a is not the source analysis. The page also records historical inattention and numb-limb uses.

freshPages.summary: The adjective normally does not precede a noun. Separate senses cover sleeping and a numb body part. The entry supports fall asleep, fast/sound asleep and figurative asleep on the job/at the wheel for inattention to responsibilities. Literal sleeping while driving remains possible and must be distinguished by context.
